evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: By definition, aphasia is not present in people with PPAOS at the time of initial diagnosis. It may not emerge for several years, may remain mild once it does, and with progression the AOS usually remains predominant.

nodes.description: Dysarthric speech (often spastic or hypokinetic) frequently emerges as the neurodegenerative syndrome progresses.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: Dysarthria can be present but cannot be more severe than the AOS at presentation.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: Dysarthria frequently develops in PPAOS, although it nearly always remains less severe than the AOS. Overall, it was present at initial assessment in 30% of PPAOS cases in our current research cohort.

nodes.description: Swallowing impairment with choking occurs frequently as patients evolve toward a PSP-like syndrome.

nodes.description: Parkinsonian/extrapyramidal motor features (such as bradykinesia and rigidity) emerge during disease progression in virtually all longitudinally followed patients.

evidence.reference_title: The evolution of primary progressive apraxia of speech.

nodes.description: Most autopsied PPAOS cases are caused by an underlying 4-repeat (4R) tauopathy, most commonly corticobasal degeneration (CBD) or progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), which drives neuronal and glial tau inclusion formation and initiates selective neurodegeneration in premotor and supplementary motor speech cortices. A minority of patients show Pick disease (3R tau) or non-tau / Alzheimer disease biomarker profiles, though isolated AOS at onset remains most strongly predictive of 4R tauopathy.

evidence.reference_title: Amyloid and Tau PET Positivity in Progressive Agrammatic Aphasia and Apraxia of Speech.
evidence.snippet: These patients typically have an underlying 4-repeat tauopathy, although they sometimes show evidence of amyloid-β and tau deposition on PET, suggesting Alzheimer's disease (AD).

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: Most published autopsied cases with an initial PPAOS diagnosis have had a 4-repeat (4R) tauopathy (a subcategory of proteinopathies), with CBD and PSP being the most common PPAOS-associated disease subtypes (e.g., (Boeve et al., 2003; Gorno-Tempini et al., 2011; Josephs et al., 2005; Josephs & Duffy, 2008; Josephs et al., 2016; Tetzloff, Duffy, Strand, et al., 2018)). A few cases have had Pick disease pathology (a 3R tauopathy), or even non-tau pathology, but it is uncertain if the AOS was the only speech, language or nonaphasic-cognitive disorder at onset in those cases (Botha & Josephs, 2019).

nodes.description: Focal grey-matter atrophy, cortical hypometabolism, and white-matter tract degeneration of the superior lateral premotor cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), and superior longitudinal fasciculus impair the planning, sequencing, and programming of articulatory motor commands.
nodes.id: Premotor and Supplementary Motor Cortex Degeneration

evidence.reference_title: Characterizing a neurodegenerative syndrome: primary progressive apraxia of speech.
evidence.snippet: Voxel-based morphometry of grey matter revealed focal atrophy of superior lateral premotor cortex and supplementary motor area.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: Studies consistently point to grey and white matter involvement in cortical and subcortical regions that are linked to speech planning/programming, production, and monitoring. The brunt of cortical abnormalities usually are in the superior lateral premotor area and SMA of the left or left greater than right hemisphere, with white matter loss extending to the inferior premotor cortex and body of the corpus callosum.

nodes.description: Impaired planning and programming of speech movements produces distorted, effortful, or segmented speech and is the obligate initial defining feature of PPAOS.

evidence.reference_title: Characterizing a neurodegenerative syndrome: primary progressive apraxia of speech.
evidence.snippet: Apraxia of speech is a disorder of speech motor planning and/or programming that is distinguishable from aphasia and dysarthria.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: PPAOS can be more narrowly defined as AOS of insidious onset and gradual progression, in the absence of more than equivocal evidence of aphasia, nonaphasic cognitive impairments or sensorimotor deficits that meet criteria for another specific neurodegenerative disease or other explanatory condition at the time of diagnosis.

nodes.description: Behavioral speech-language intervention, compensatory strategies, and augmentative and alternative communication are used to maintain functional communication, although PPAOS-specific treatment evidence remains limited.

evidence.reference_title: Behavioral Treatment for Speech and Language in Primary Progressive Aphasia and Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: The available evidence supports speech-language intervention for persons with PPA; however, treatment for PPAOS awaits systematic investigation.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: Beyond efforts to maintain or improve speech, staging of management to develop effective speaker and listener compensatory strategies, with early and ongoing involvement of partners, preferably in advance of reduced intelligibility, are essential and achievable in many cases.

nodes.description: Over ~5 years of longitudinal progression, accelerated atrophy, white-matter tract degeneration, and hypometabolism spread from the premotor cortex and SMA into the basal ganglia, thalamus, midbrain, motor cortex white matter, and left inferior frontal lobe, driving the emergence of extrapyramidal motor signs, bulbar dysphagia, and late-onset nonfluent aphasia.
nodes.id: Subcortical, Brainstem, and Perisylvian Network Spread

evidence.reference_title: The evolution of primary progressive apraxia of speech.
evidence.snippet: Increased rates of brain atrophy over time were observed throughout the premotor cortex, as well as prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, basal ganglia and midbrain, while white matter tract degeneration spread into the splenium of the corpus callosum and motor cortex white matter.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: From Recognition to Diagnosis and Care.
evidence.snippet: Longitudinal imaging demonstrates increased atrophy and hypometabolism in the same regions, with spread into the left inferior frontal lobe, basal ganglia and thalamus in those who develop aphasia over time.
